content:
Last time we talked about KingSir's 1987 translation and direction of *Cyrano de Bergerac*, in which the gifted and proud Cyrano faced his beloved cousin Roxane with cowardice and self-abasement. When I interviewed Anthony Wong in 2015, I asked him:

"Actually, does a man's talent make him feel inferior because of his big nose?"

"The moment love comes along, yes. Normally he wouldn't, but once love enters the picture, he becomes a fragile little boy. Love is something very childish." (audio clip)

Precisely because of a nose so different from everyone else's, Cyrano felt inferior. Love sometimes makes people vulnerable, only accepting their strengths, never their weaknesses — this is human nature, and it is also dramatic. Both life and drama need sublimation. Anthony Wong said this was France's last Romanticist play. An ugly man writing love letters for a handsome man to the woman he loves — much like so much in the world, where appearance and truth are always intertwined, ever so false yet not without sincerity. What the woman loves is the soul poured into those words and madly loving her, though she always believed that person was the handsome Christian. How is the truth finally revealed?

Anthony Wong explained the backstory: "After Cyrano was ambushed and injured in the head, he still visited his cousin every week. His cousin didn't know he deeply loved her. He wrote letters on behalf of the handsome man to court his cousin. Just as that handsome man wanted to confess that he hadn't written the letters — because the woman said she loved his talent — at the very moment of his confession, Christian was shot dead on the battlefield. His cousin then took the letters and retreated into a convent. Cyrano would visit every week, sharing news and small talk to cheer her up. When he was about to die, as darkness fell, he asked his cousin to read the letter to him again. As she read on, before she needed to read further, he recited it from memory. How could he know it by heart? It was at that moment his cousin finally realised that this was the same voice she had heard on the balcony all those years ago. Only then did she discover it was him."

Is half of life's most beautiful stories a lie?

The handsome Christian, trying to put pen to paper on the battlefield to clarify the truth, was shot dead, his blood staining the letter; the tears upon it were Cyrano's. Blood and tears are both real, and their coexistence does not mean they came from the same man. In life's good and bad, if you refuse to take them both in, in the end, you may lose them all. "Each of us has our own wound" — when I read the final scene of the original, Cyrano, after being ambushed in the head, arrives gravely wounded at the convent to find his cousin Roxane. Roxane notices his injury, and Cyrano lies to her that it is an old wound. He then touches upon his own pain: "Each of us has our own wound, and so do I. That old wound of mine has never healed."

He takes from his chest the love letter stained with blood and tears — the letter she had believed was written to her by Christian. She agrees to let Cyrano read it. Here, Cyrano holds the love letter and begins to recite: "Goodbye, Roxane, I am about to die. The love I never spoke weighs so heavily upon my soul. My eyes will no longer be able to revel in your every little movement. I miss the way, when you speak, you gently touch your cheek with your fingers — a gesture so familiar to me. Deep in my heart I am crying out: farewell!"

"You can read that letter so well, as if..." Roxane.

"My life, my love, my treasure, my beloved — my heart has always been hidden within every beat of yours."

After darkness falls in the convent, Cyrano could not possibly see the contents of the letter — this is the dramatic flaw. And yet, his familiar voice reading the love letter allows Roxane to recognise the voice of the soul she had always loved:

"That person was you!"

"No, Roxane, no!"

"Every time you called my name, I should have known."

"No, that wasn't me!" "That was you!" "I swear!"

"I now see that generous lie clearly — those love letters were from you!"

"No!"

"Those sweet words, that mad love. It was all you!"

"No!"

"That voice that shook me in the darkness!"

"I swear, you are mistaken!"

"That soul — it was yours!"

"I never loved you!" "You loved me!"

"No, that was him!"

"You loved me!"

"No!" (his voice weakening)

"Your voice is trembling; the force of your denial grows softer!"

Drama is loving someone, unable to speak it, left only with the word "no" — the more one speaks, the weaker one becomes, the more one's heart panics. Drama is loving someone, unable to confess, one's whole life twisted and turned. Drama is loving someone, even when you cannot be together, yet through words and soul finding a way to love deeply. Drama is a lifetime spent wrestling with joy and pain, falsehood and truth. When Roxane discovers that the author of the love letters is the dying Cyrano, she says: "I loved a man, yet I lost him twice."

Life slips away without our knowledge or control. Two men who love her, neither can have her — this is drama. She truly loved a soul, yet lost him twice: once when Christian died in battle; and once when, upon discovering Cyrano was the true author of the letters, Cyrano died in her arms. Dialogue like poetry — that too is drama.

"The final lines are wonderful too. As I pass through the threshold of God, I will sweep all the stars from the lintel, and the only thing unstained is my glorious white plume. So dignified." (Anthony Wong audio)

A Lifetime of Yearning — The World of Drama

Watching King Sir's *Cyrano de Bergerac* in its final scene back then, in a pitch-dark theatre, I sat in the middle-front, as if I alone were witnessing the end of the world, freely moved, emotions churning within. Returning to my own heart, what life ultimately needs, and what it possesses day by day, are always worlds apart. *Cyrano de Bergerac* brought the essence of tragedy to life through humour: precious. A lifetime of yearning and a lifetime of seeking — that is life. Thoughts are free. Beyond being moved and touched, I came to understand, on my own, that a lesson in drama can change one's mind and thinking, reveal another world, and beyond performance, allow one to find the source of that world.

What is a theatre? In that moment, it was a place in the darkness where I looked forward to the future. It doesn't have to be acting, but one must earnestly pursue the highest good and beauty. Missing out on the academy, losing something, is in fact moving towards another possibility. What matters most is that you still know what you want.

King Sir's stage productions opened my eyes. Another of his early works at the Academy, *Under the Banyan Tree*, was also a brilliant original play with strong local Hong Kong character. In junior secondary, I heard about his productions of *The Horse*, *The Death of Mozart*, *Death of a Salesman* and *West Side Story*, among others — none of which I ever got to see. Even more regrettably, I never had the chance to discuss a life in drama with King Sir. Over a decade ago, through the late PolyU PR officer Lai Ming-fai, I sat in on King Sir's auditions for a drama performance at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. Afterwards, I politely introduced myself and personally requested an interview. King Sir at the time remained as friendly and gentle as he had been decades earlier when selecting APA applicants, but regarding my interview request, he politely declined in a rather evasive manner.

"Whether with peers or with young people, he was always humble and wore a smile. This was not acting, but the sincere understanding of a gentleman who knew how to make people feel respected and at ease."

In the 2018 English citation for Shue Yan University conferring an honorary doctorate upon Mr King Sir, I particularly agreed with the above. From my own encounter with King Sir, his smile and the look in his eyes as he regarded you made you feel respected, and your heart warmed. I personally suspect that his refusal for an interview was related to the tensions between the television station and the newspaper I belonged to at the time.

Back then, when I wanted to study at the Academy, people assumed I dreamed of becoming an actor, of performing. I immediately replied: "No, I want to study drama." That might mean directing, or playwriting, or the world of literature. From junior secondary onwards, I wrote two or three scripts, self-directed and self-acted, but the passion ultimately faded, buried quietly in my heart — once a lingering regret.

Four years ago, when writing the Dickens readings for my Patreon, I read several related academic articles and came to understand how Dickens evolved from missing his chance to be an actor and journalist into becoming a literary giant. My view of long-held dreams was renewed.

In his later years, Dickens performed readings of his own works — self-written, self-directed live readings — whose ticket revenue exceeded that of his novels, and more than half his wealth came from this (see the first Patreon article). He transformed the performing passion of his youth into readings of his own works. The wonder of life does not lie solely in realising dreams, but in transformation and sublimation. The greatest drama lesson in life is called *blessing in disguise*. Sometimes love cannot be attained, but if one makes good use of what one already holds, amid countless transformations, with love remaining in one's heart, one can ultimately reach the same destination by another path.

Last year in England, I walked around Dickens's former home in Rochester. It is said that Dickens's father once encouraged his son to strive upwards so that one day he might buy such a house. Dickens did indeed buy this house, and it still stands today, connected to a secondary school — how fortunate the students are.

Life is like a play; there is no need to lament its twists and turns, for there are far too many possibilities worth admiring. Once I understood this, I channelled my passion into free self-expression, becoming a journalist who loves writing about people. I pour the most emotion into true stories, stories that contain you, me, and him — one after another "text-based stage plays". If they can move people, that is the warmest applause.

The Beginnings and Golden Years of the Academy — The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts has been established for over forty years. At its founding, it had only four schools: Drama, Music, Dance, and Theatre Technology (Technical Arts). Later, Film & Television and Chinese Opera were added, making six. Looking back at this academy I could not enter, in the mid-eighties, no university campus could be so magnificent and elegant, with air-conditioning available around the clock. To maintain the venue and equipment, every corner was kept chillingly cool. The brand-new carpets in alternating green and purple were harmonious in colour, yet psychologically gave one a sense of abstract dizziness. At every performance, the hall was filled with distinguished Chinese and foreign officials and business guests — a scene of flourishing splendour. That was the initial stage when Hong Kong's performing arts entered the halls of academia. With student participation, a bottom-up freedom in the arts took shape, and it was also the freest and most glorious era for Hong Kong's performing arts — without class distinction, allowing students and scholars alike to give full rein to their talents.

In the first few years after its founding, for various reasons, I often wandered through the countless corners of this "great playground". To be honest, when I first walked in, I felt very small and out of place — not because it was grand, but because the atmosphere was so detached from the everyday of our lives, yet accessible to everyone. Students from different backgrounds and classes came together to learn, united by shared interests and ideals. It was a very special yet somehow not so difficult existence.

Whether King King-fai is a master depends on whether we have inherited an environment that nurtures a master. The Academy has developed for forty-two years; Hong Kong has built a system and standards for the performing arts. The culture of drama, apart from blooming through various theatre companies, has also taken root and grown within the freedom of academia. King King-fai is a foundational landmark. From his era onward, many professional theatre practitioners dedicated to drama education, together with their students, generation after generation — able to perform and to teach — Hong Kong's dramatic performing arts was entering a period of diverse blossoming and fruition. It is easy to build a grand building, but difficult to produce a master. Hong Kong is a society that anticipates masters; the focus is not only on achievements, but on a free framework that can continue to pass down and nurture talent.
